title: India's Youth Unemployment Climbs to 15 Per Cent — The Highest in Over a Decade
excerpt: Government data reveals a deepening jobs crisis among 15-29-year-olds, raising uncomfortable questions about the country's demographic dividend
body:
India's promise to its young people has always rested on a simple bargain: stay, study, and the jobs will come. That bargain is fraying.

Unemployment among Indians aged 15-29 rose to 15 per cent in the January-March 2026 quarter, up from 14.3 per cent in the previous quarter, according to data released by the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI). The figure represents the highest youth joblessness rate recorded in over a decade, and it arrives at a moment when India's leaders have been trumpeting the country's demographic dividend — the notion that a young, growing workforce will power the next phase of economic expansion.

The numbers paint a particularly stark picture for young women. Female youth unemployment climbed to 17.7 per cent during the same period, according to NDTV's analysis of the data, while male youth unemployment stood at 14.3 per cent. Labour force participation among women aged 15-29 dropped to 22.3 per cent by March 2026, suggesting that millions of young Indian women have simply stopped looking for work.

## The Paradox of Education

Perhaps the most troubling aspect of the data is its relationship with education. In most economies, higher qualifications translate into lower unemployment. In India, the relationship has inverted. Graduates and postgraduates face *higher* unemployment rates than those with only secondary education — a pattern the National Council of Applied Economic Research (NCAER) has described as a "qualification trap."

The explanation lies in the mismatch between what Indian universities produce and what the economy demands. Engineering colleges churn out roughly 1.5 million graduates annually, but the IT sector — long the primary absorber of technical talent — has slowed hiring dramatically as automation and artificial intelligence reduce the need for entry-level roles. The result is a growing population of educated, aspirational, and increasingly frustrated young Indians.

"India's 11.6 million unemployed young adults face extended job searches due to AI-driven labour market mismatches," NCAER noted in a recent analysis. States like Rajasthan and Bihar show particularly high unemployment among youth, while Kerala's gender gap highlights how regional disparities compound the national crisis.

## The Structural Problem

India's overall unemployment rate remains modest at 5 per cent, which the government frequently cites as evidence of a healthy labour market. But that headline figure obscures a structural reality: much of India's employment is in the informal sector, characterised by low wages, no benefits, and zero job security. The Employees' Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) data, which tracks formal-sector jobs, tells a less encouraging story about the quality of employment being created.

The manufacturing sector, which was expected to absorb millions of workers through initiatives like 'Make in India,' has added jobs at a pace well below targets. Rural employment, meanwhile, is shifting away from agriculture — the traditional fallback — toward secondary and tertiary sectors, but not quickly enough to absorb the workers being displaced.

## The Diaspora Connection

For the Indian diaspora, these numbers are more than statistics. They represent younger siblings, cousins, and the children of friends struggling to find their footing in an economy that was supposed to offer them the world.

The youth unemployment crisis is also the primary engine of the brain drain that feeds the diaspora itself. Every year, hundreds of thousands of young Indians pursue degrees abroad — not purely for the education, but because the foreign degree serves as an exit visa from a job market that cannot accommodate them. The H-1B visa programme, student visas to the UK, Canada, and Australia, and increasingly creative pathways to the Gulf — all of these are symptoms of the same disease.

Indian families abroad pour money into educating relatives back home, often with the expectation that the investment will yield a stable career. When it doesn't, the pressure shifts: the relative needs help coming abroad, the cycle of sponsorship and immigration begins again, and the demographic dividend that was supposed to keep India's young at home instead propels them outward.

## What Needs to Change

Economists and policy analysts have called for a fundamental rethink of India's approach to employment. The NCAER recommends developing new competencies like "resourcefulness and integrative thinking" rather than narrow technical skills. Others have called for a massive expansion of apprenticeship programmes and a closer alignment between university curricula and industry needs.

But the clock is ticking. India's demographic window — the period when the working-age population exceeds dependents — will begin closing by the mid-2030s. If the country cannot create meaningful employment for its young before then, the dividend becomes a liability, and the world's largest youth population transforms from an asset into a crisis.
